Hewers
HYOO-erz
n. pl.
From Old English heawan, to cut or strike with an edged tool. Webster 1828: one who cuts wood or stone. In Scripture the hewers are the lowest rank of the labour force, and the phrase hewers of wood and drawers of water has passed from Joshua 9 into English as the standing name for the humblest work.

Biblical Definition

The hewers enter Scripture through the Gibeonites’ deceit. Having tricked Israel into a league with mouldy bread and clouted shoes, they were found out, and Joshua could not break an oath sworn by the LORD. So the princes ruled: Let them live; but let them be hewers of wood and drawers of water unto all the congregation (Joshua 9:21). Joshua added the detail that turned the sentence into a mercy: it was for the congregation, and for the altar of the LORD, even unto this day, in the place which he should choose (Joshua 9:27). A people under the ban became servants of the sanctuary and lived beside the altar for centuries; they are still there in Nehemiah’s day as the Nethinim. Solomon set fourscore thousand hewers in the mountain for the temple (2 Chronicles 2:18). The word turns dark only once, and it is the greatest of the prophetic indictments: my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water (Jeremiah 2:13). There the hewing is man’s own labour to secure what God was already giving freely, and every stroke of the chisel was wasted.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines HEWER as one who hews wood or stone, and HEW as to cut with an axe or other instrument, and to form or shape with a cutting tool. The scriptural phrase hewers of wood and drawers of water he treats as proverbial for the meanest service.

expand to see more

HEWER, n. — One who hews wood or stone.

HEW, v.t. — To cut with an axe or other sharp instrument; to chop; to fell.

To form or shape with a cutting instrument; as, to hew a stone, to hew out a sepulchre.

Hewers of wood and drawers of water — proverbially, those who perform the meanest offices; from Joshua 9:21.

Deuteronomy 29:11 shows the phrase was already a settled expression for the lowest station within the covenant assembly.

Key Scripture

Joshua 9:21 — "And the princes said unto them, Let them live; but let them be hewers of wood and drawers of water unto all the congregation; as the princes had promised them."

Joshua 9:27 — "And Joshua made them that day hewers of wood and drawers of water for the congregation, and for the altar of the LORD, even unto this day, in the place which he should choose."

2 Chronicles 2:18 — "And he set threescore and ten thousand of them to be bearers of burdens, and fourscore thousand to be hewers in the mountain, and three thousand and six hundred overseers to set the people a work."

Jeremiah 2:13 — "For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water."

Deuteronomy 29:11 — "Your little ones, your wives, and thy stranger that is in thy camp, from the hewer of thy wood unto the drawer of thy water:"

Modern Corruption

Jeremiah 2:13 is the definitive statement of what every false religion and every self-made righteousness actually is: not the rejection of water, but the substitution of hard, cracked, self-quarried tanks for a living spring.

expand to see more

Two evils, and the prophet numbers them. The first is forsaking the fountain of living waters — a spring that runs without being worked, that costs nothing, that is simply there. The second is the labour of hewing cisterns out of rock, which in Judah’s limestone required weeks of chiselling and then plastering, and which cracked and lost the water anyway. That is the anatomy of works-righteousness, and it explains why it is so hard to abandon: the cistern represents effort, and a man will not easily walk away from something he has cut out of stone with his own hands. Every system of religion that requires a man to produce his own standing before God is a cistern, and Jeremiah’s point is that they all leak.

The Gibeonite sentence teaches the complementary lesson, and it is a gentler one. They lied to save their lives and were sentenced to perpetual menial service, and the sentence put them beside the altar of the LORD for the rest of Israel’s history. Centuries later, when Saul slew them in his zeal, God sent a three-year famine on Israel for it (2 Samuel 21:1) — the Judge of all the earth defending a people who had entered the covenant by fraud, because Israel had sworn. God keeps oaths sworn in His name even when the swearing was foolish, and He has a habit of making the lowest place in His house better than the highest place outside it. I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chatab (H2404), to cut or gather wood, whence hewers of wood; chatsab (H2672), to hew or quarry stone, the verb of Jeremiah 2:13.

expand to see more

Hebrew chatab (H2404) — to cut wood, to gather firewood; hewers of wood (Joshua 9:21).

Hebrew chatsab (H2672) — to hew, to quarry, to dig out; hewed them out cisterns (Jeremiah 2:13).

Hebrew bor (H953) — a cistern, a pit; the hewn tank that will not hold water.

Hebrew mayim chayyim — living waters, that is, running spring water as opposed to stored water.

Hebrew Nethinim (H5411) — the given ones; the temple servants of Ezra and Nehemiah, traditionally traced to the Gibeonites.

Usage

"Let them be hewers of wood and drawers of water (Joshua 9:21) — a sentence that became a place beside the altar."

"Fourscore thousand to be hewers in the mountain (2 Chronicles 2:18) — the labour behind the temple’s stone."

"Hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns (Jeremiah 2:13) — the exhausting industry of works-righteousness."
